focus: D2L scales its per-example loss by 1/2 while HoML differentiates the plain mean of squares with a 2/m gradient. The minimizer is identical but the largest stable learning rate differs by that constant.
X'Xw = X'y has a unique solution only when X has full column rank. With duplicate or collinear columns the fitted values stay unique but the coefficients do not.
The course notebooks show inv(X'X)@X'y to teach the formula; sklearn never forms that inverse and solves through the SVD instead.
units.reproduce: From ||y - Xw||^2, derive X'Xw = X'y on paper. Then in NumPy with default_rng(1) on the correlated demo (n = 200, x2 = x1 + 1e-4 noise): show cond(X'X) = 4.335643e+08 equals cond(X) squared, and lstsq matches the explicit-inverse coefficients to 4 decimals. With default_rng(0) and 1e-8 noise, show the explicit inverse reaches residual 3.8314 while lstsq reaches 3.7978.
traps: Shipping inv(X'X)@X'y as the solver. Forming X'X squares the condition number, so a design with cond(X) near 1e8 makes X'X numerically singular near 1/eps in float64 while lstsq still minimizes the residual.
Hand-rolling a bias column while the differential test keeps fit_intercept=True. That fits two offsets and the comparison fails for no mathematical reason.

Reading the second Deep-ML 15 test as the exact solution. It expects [2.9699, 2.0078], the gradient-descent iterate after 1000 steps at lr 0.05; the exact minimizer is [3, 2]. Zero initialization and the exact update decide it.

selfTest.q: D2L multiplies its loss by 1/2 and HoML does not. Why is the minimizer unchanged but the stable learning rate different?
selfTest.a: The constant scales the loss and every gradient without moving the stationary point, so the optimum is identical. A fixed step size moves half as far per step under the 1/2 convention, so its stability limit on eta is twice as large.

selfTest.q: Two columns of X are identical. What happens to X'X, the coefficients and the predictions?
selfTest.a: X'X is singular so the coefficients are not unique. The fitted values Xw stay unique as the projection onto the column space, and SVD-based solvers return the minimum-norm coefficient vector.

selfTest.q: cond(X) is 2.08e4. What is cond(X'X), and at what point does the explicit inverse break down?
selfTest.a: About 4.34e8, the square of cond(X). The explicit inverse loses all precision once cond(X'X) approaches 1/eps, about 4.5e15 in float64, which needs only cond(X) near 1e8.

selfTest.q: One label is corrupted upward by 100. Why does the squared-loss fit move far, and which single change to the loss limits the damage?
selfTest.a: The quadratic penalty lets that one residual dominate the objective. An absolute-error loss grows only linearly with it, so the fit moves far less.

focus: Ridge alpha multiplies an unnormalized RSS while Lasso and ElasticNet alphas multiply a 1/(2n) mean loss, so alpha = 1 means different strengths. Compare paths or CV errors, never raw alphas.
Penalties tax raw coefficient size, so a feature in small units pays more than the same signal in large units. Standardize slopes before penalizing and leave the intercept free.

Lasso lands on corners and selects one of a correlated pair almost arbitrarily while elastic net keeps both. D2L's d = 200, n = 20 demo shows weight decay rescuing a fit with more features than samples.
units.reproduce: Derive w = (X'X + alpha I)^{-1} X'y for centered data. With default_rng(2) on the correlated demo (n = 100, x3 = x1 + 0.1 noise), show Ridge(alpha=1.0) equals the closed form to 1e-14 at [1.33909931, -3.06183881, 0.64520852]; show Lasso(alpha=100.0) returns all zeros while Ridge at any finite alpha keeps every coefficient nonzero.
traps: Judging Ridge(alpha=1) against Lasso(alpha=1) as a fair fight. The objectives normalize the loss differently, so match effective shrinkage or validation error instead.
Fitting the scaler on all the data, or penalizing the intercept. Fit standardization on train only and keep the offset out of the penalty.
Reading lasso zeros as proof the dropped features carry no signal. Across resamples a correlated rival is selected instead, so report selection stability rather than one mask.

selfTest.q: Ridge(alpha=1) and Lasso(alpha=1) disagree sharply on standardized data. Is one implementation wrong?
selfTest.a: No. Ridge adds alpha times the raw RSS while Lasso adds alpha times the mean-scaled loss, so the same number applies different pressure. Sweep a path and compare by validation error.

selfTest.q: D2L 3.7 fits d = 200 features on 20 examples. Why does plain least squares break, and what does the L2 term change algebraically?
selfTest.a: X'X is rank-deficient, so infinitely many weight vectors fit training exactly. Adding alpha I makes X'X + alpha I full rank and selects the small-norm solution.

selfTest.q: Two features correlate at 0.999. Lasso keeps one with a large weight while ridge keeps both, shrunken. Why?
selfTest.a: The L1 constraint is a diamond with corners on the axes, so loss contours first touch at a sparse point. The L2 ball is round and strictly convex, so it splits weight across correlated directions.

selfTest.q: A degree-n polynomial on distinct x values fits training data perfectly. Is it the best model?
selfTest.a: No. Zero training error does not imply low validation error: the exact-fit polynomial oscillates between points. That gap is what the underfitting-overfitting curve diagnoses.

study.locator: Estimating Probabilities (iris virginica detector on petal width) and Decision Boundaries (boundary contour with C = 2)

focus: The gradient is prediction error times input, summed over rows. Mitchell ascends the log likelihood from zero weights while sklearn minimizes averaged cross-entropy with lbfgs, so their paths differ while their optima agree.
sklearn regularizes by default at C = 1.0 on an averaged loss, so its C is not a textbook lambda: smaller C means stronger penalty, and C = inf recovers the unpenalized fit.
Never exponentiate before logging. Sigmoid saturates to exactly 0 or 1 beyond about |z| = 710 in float64, and -log(0) is inf; the form max(z,0) - z y + log1p(exp(-|z|)) stays finite.
units.reproduce: Derive the (p - y) x gradient from the binary log likelihood. In float64 show the naive loss returns inf for (z = -800, y = 1) while max(z,0) - z y + log1p(exp(-|z|)) returns 800.0, and match your analytic gradient to central differences to 1e-8 on a 3-point demo.
traps: Equating sklearn C with a textbook lambda. C is inverse strength on an averaged loss, so doubling C halves the penalty; sample and class weights rescale the effective C through the total weight S.
Trusting probabilities from a near-unpenalized fit on nearly separable data. The likelihood keeps rewarding larger weights, so scores saturate toward exactly 0 and 1 without becoming more accurate.

Starting gradient ascent from large random weights for symmetry breaking. The objective is concave with one global optimum and Mitchell starts at zero; large starts only waste steps or overflow the first sigmoid.

selfTest.q: Why does logistic regression need iterative fitting when linear regression has a closed form?
selfTest.a: The sigmoid makes the log likelihood nonlinear in w with no analytic maximizer. The objective is concave, so gradient ascent still reaches the one global optimum.

selfTest.q: sklearn at default C = 1.0 disagrees with your zero-penalty NumPy fit. Which one is right?
selfTest.a: Both solve their stated objectives: sklearn minimizes averaged cross-entropy plus an L2 term at C = 1.0. Set C to inf or a very large value to recover the unpenalized fit.

selfTest.q: Training loss prints inf on the first epoch with a logit near -800. What happened, and what is the fix?
selfTest.a: Sigmoid saturated to exactly 0 and log(0) is inf. Score in logits with max(z,0) - z y + log1p(exp(-|z|)) instead of exponentiating first.

selfTest.q: Recompute ISLP's 58.6% default risk for balance $2,000 from Table 4.1.
selfTest.a: z = -10.6513 + 0.0055 x 2000 = 0.3487; 1/(1 + exp(-0.3487)) = 0.586. A one-unit balance rise adds 0.0055 to the log odds.

study.title: One-versus-rest in practice
study.locator: Multiclass Classification section: the SVC OvO-training note, OneVsRestClassifier with its 10 estimators, and the SGDClassifier multiclass run

focus: Softmax preserves order, so argmax needs no exponentials. Probabilities still need the max-subtracted form, because exp(1000) overflows to inf and inf divided by inf is nan.
sklearn fits K vectors for K classes on purpose, for symmetry under regularization. Without penalty that redundancy makes the solution non-unique, which is one more reason the default L2 matters.
One-versus-rest trains K binary problems and compares uncalibrated margins, while multinomial optimizes one joint loss. Expect worse-calibrated probabilities from the OvR scheme.
units.reproduce: Derive the (p_k - y_k) x gradient from the multiclass negative log likelihood. In NumPy show naive softmax of [1000, 1001, 999] returns [nan, nan, nan] while the max-subtracted form returns [0.2447, 0.6652, 0.0900]; then solve the D2L 4.4 exercise by fixing inputs whose largest value sits below -100.
traps: Copying the D2L 4.4 teaching softmax into real code. The page itself warns against verbatim use; framework implementations subtract the row maximum internally.
Calling OvR margins probabilities. One-versus-rest decision_function scores are not calibrated across the K classifiers; take predict_proba from a joint fit or calibrate afterwards.
Passing multi_class to LogisticRegression under sklearn 1.9. The parameter is removed and raises TypeError; OvR now means the liblinear solver or an explicit OneVsRestClassifier.

selfTest.q: Why can argmax skip the softmax entirely?
selfTest.a: Softmax is monotone in each logit and preserves their order, so the largest logit is always the most probable class. Computing probabilities still needs the stable form.

selfTest.q: sklearn fits 3 vectors for 3 classes while Mitchell fits K - 1 = 2 linear functions. Is one of them wrong?
selfTest.a: No. K vectors deliberately overparameterize for symmetry under regularization, while K - 1 suffices because probabilities sum to one. Without penalty the K-vector solution is not unique.

selfTest.q: Naive softmax of [1000, 1001, 999] returns nan. Show the exact failure and the fix.
selfTest.a: Each exponential overflows to inf and inf/inf is nan. Subtract the row maximum first: exp([-1, 0, -2]) over its sum gives [0.2447, 0.6652, 0.0900] with the same argmax.

selfTest.q: liblinear is your only allowed solver on a 5-class problem. Which scheme, and what do you lose?
selfTest.a: One-versus-rest, for example OneVsRestClassifier with 5 binary estimators. You lose the joint multinomial objective and should expect worse-calibrated probabilities.

units.why: A fit that converges is not a fit that is right. Diagnostics separate a broken model from a broken assumption, and separation is the one failure that looks like perfect success.

focus: Leverage measures position in x-space, not wrongness. The x = 10 point in a 0-to-2 design carries leverage 0.98 out of p = 2 while anchoring the slope; residuals measure wrongness, and influence needs both.

Patterns have signatures. Curvature in residual-versus-fitted means nonlinearity, a funnel means heteroscedasticity, and isolated large standardized residuals mean outliers; each prescribes a different repair.

Separation shows as coefficients that grow every time C is relaxed (0.96 at C = 1, 9.31 at C = 1e3, 16.57 at C = 1e6 on the x = 0,1,2,3 demo) with probabilities glued to 0 and 1. The fix is a finite penalty, not more iterations.
units.reproduce: From a blank file compute hat diagonals on the design [[1,0],[1,1],[1,2],[1,10]] and match leverages [0.4183, 0.3307, 0.2749, 0.9761] summing to p = 2. Then fit LogisticRegression at C = 1, 1e3 and 1e6 on x = [0,1,2,3] with y = [0,0,1,1] and match single-feature coefficients [0.9583], [9.3057] and [16.5719] with probabilities saturating toward 0 and 1.
traps: Deleting every high-leverage point. Leverage is not guilt: a far-x point with a small residual anchors the fit. Act on influence, residuals times leverage, not on position alone.

Reading saturated 0 and 1 probabilities as a great classifier. Under separation the likelihood rewards ever-larger weights, so perfect scores signal an unidentified model rather than a solved problem.
Raising max_iter or C to force a separated fit to converge. Extra iterations only grow the weights further; keep the penalty finite or collect overlapping cases, and confirm the weights stop growing.

selfTest.q: Residual-versus-fitted shows a U shape. What is wrong, and what changes?
selfTest.a: Nonlinearity the linear form cannot express. Add polynomial or interaction terms rather than collecting more data for the same line.

selfTest.q: The x = 10 point has leverage 0.98 out of p = 2. Should it be deleted?
selfTest.a: Not on leverage alone. It dominates the slope estimate but a small residual there is informative. Check influence by refitting without it before deciding.

selfTest.q: Logistic coefficients grow tenfold each time C grows tenfold, and every probability prints as 0 or 1. Diagnose and repair.
selfTest.a: Complete separation: the maximum likelihood weights are unbounded and only the penalty keeps them finite. Keep C finite, confirm the weights stabilize, and look for overlapping cases to collect.

selfTest.q: Standardized residuals fan out as fitted values grow. Name the violation and one valid response.
selfTest.a: Heteroscedasticity, non-constant error variance. Transform the response, model the variance, or use variance-robust inference; adding polynomial terms does not fix it.

study.locator: Section 1.2.2 (Bayes rule, Gaussian class conditionals, QDA log-posterior, LDA linear form with coef_ and intercept_, and the QDA-with-diagonal-covariance equals GaussianNB note) and 1.2.5 (svd is the default solver)

study.title: LDA and QDA lab on the Smarket data
study.locator: Linear Discriminant Analysis and Quadratic Discriminant Analysis sections: fits, posterior values and confusion matrices beside the logistic fit

focus: LDA log odds are linear in x because the shared covariance cancels every quadratic term; QDA keeps one covariance per class, so its boundary is quadratic with cross terms.

Gaussian naive Bayes is QDA with diagonal covariances, and one-dimensional Gaussian naive Bayes with shared variances is LDA with diagonal shared covariance. Neither method subsumes the other in general: naive Bayes is purely additive while QDA multiplies features.

Logistic regression and LDA posit the same linear log-odds form but fit it differently: LDA estimates class Gaussians and priors while logistic maximizes the conditional likelihood. Expect LDA to win when normality holds and logistic when it does not.
units.reproduce: Write the LDA discriminant delta_k(x) = x' Sigma^{-1} mu_k - mu_k' Sigma^{-1} mu_k / 2 + log pi_k from the Gaussian log posterior. On the two-Gaussian demo (40 points per class, means [0,0] and [2,2], default_rng(3)), match sklearn LDA priors [0.5, 0.5], score 0.95, coefficients [1.927, 2.229] and intercept -4.070.
traps: Fitting QDA with fewer samples than features per class. Each class covariance needs its own estimate from its own rows; with n below p per class the matrix is singular and LDA with shrinkage is the honest fallback.
Calling LDA parameter-free. It exposes no tuning knob by default but still estimates K means, a shared covariance and priors, which overfit small samples.

Assuming discriminative always wins with enough data. Logistic wins asymptotically under misspecification, but the generative fit converges in O(log n) versus O(n) examples, so LDA and naive Bayes often win when training data is scarce.

selfTest.q: Write the two-class LDA decision rule and name each estimated quantity.
selfTest.a: Assign argmax over k of x' Sigma^{-1} mu_k - mu_k' Sigma^{-1} mu_k/2 + log pi_k: class means, one shared covariance and priors. The x-quadratic terms cancel because Sigma is shared, leaving a linear boundary.

selfTest.q: When does QDA collapse to Gaussian naive Bayes, and when does Gaussian naive Bayes collapse toward LDA?
selfTest.a: QDA with diagonal class covariances is Gaussian naive Bayes. One-dimensional Gaussian naive Bayes with variances shared across classes is LDA with diagonal shared covariance. In general neither subsumes the other.

selfTest.q: 50 training points, 20 features, roughly Gaussian classes. LDA, QDA or logistic first?
selfTest.a: LDA, possibly with shrinkage. QDA must estimate two 20-by-20 covariances from about 25 points each, and logistic fits 21 weights discriminatively with higher variance. Revisit logistic if normality is badly violated and more data arrives.

selfTest.q: State the Ng and Jordan sample-complexity contrast and its practical consequence.
selfTest.a: Generative naive Bayes parameters converge in order log n examples versus order n for logistic regression, so naive Bayes often wins on tiny training sets while logistic wins with abundant data under misspecification.

study.title: Gaussian naive Bayes lab on Smarket
study.locator: Naive Bayes section: GaussianNB fit on Smarket with classes_ and class_prior_ readouts

focus: Smoothing is a MAP estimate under a Dirichlet prior, not a hack. Mitchell's (count + l)/(total + lJ) at l = 1 is Laplace, and sklearn's alpha = 1.0 is the same add-one per value; without it one unseen value zeroes the whole product.

Bernoulli penalizes absent indicator features while multinomial ignores absent counts. That is why occurrence vectors can beat count vectors on short documents, and why the two models are not interchangeable.
Score in log space always. A product of 1100 halves is exactly 0.0 in float64 while the log sum stays finite at -762.46; argmax needs only the sums.
units.reproduce: Derive the MAP rule argmax_y P(y) prod_i P(x_i|y) from conditional independence. From a blank file implement Bernoulli naive Bayes with alpha = 1.0: on X = [[1,0],[1,1],[0,0],[0,1]] with y = [1,1,0,0] match sklearn feature_log_prob_ rows [-1.3863, -0.6931] for class 0 and [-0.2877, -0.6931] for class 1, predict [1] for [[1,0]], and return the majority class when trained on one class only.
traps: Feeding counts to BernoulliNB or magnitudes to a binary model without thought. BernoulliNB binarizes continuous input at binarize = 0.0 by default, silently turning magnitudes into presence flags.
Multiplying raw probabilities and comparing. Beyond underflow, one unsmoothed zero vetoes the class; sum logs and smooth first.
Reading predict_proba as calibrated confidence. The guide calls naive Bayes a bad estimator: use the scores to rank, then threshold or calibrate downstream.

selfTest.q: A test word never appeared in training. What happens with and without smoothing?
selfTest.a: Without smoothing its likelihood is 0 and the whole class product is 0 regardless of other evidence. With Laplace alpha = 1 it contributes a small nonzero factor that rarely decides the argmax alone.

selfTest.q: When does Bernoulli beat multinomial on text, and why?
selfTest.a: With occurrence vectors on short documents: Bernoulli explicitly penalizes the non-occurrence of indicator words while multinomial ignores absent counts. sklearn advises evaluating both when time permits.

selfTest.q: Write the smoothed discrete likelihood and name its prior.
selfTest.a: (count + l)/(class total + lJ): a MAP estimate under a Dirichlet prior with equal parameters, Laplace at l = 1. Priors smooth the same way with K classes in the denominator.

selfTest.q: XOR data with labels [0,1,1,0]. Does naive Bayes succeed, and which assumption fails?
selfTest.a: No. Each feature alone is uninformative about the label, so conditional independence destroys the interaction. Allowing explicit dependence between the inputs fixes it.

units.title: Probability estimates, class priors and asymmetric thresholds
outcomes: Derive the cost-optimal threshold from class probabilities and misclassification costs, and show why 0.5 is only optimal for symmetric costs.

units.why: A probability is not a decision. The same fitted scores need different thresholds under different costs and different priors, and 0.5 is a cost claim most projects never stated.

study.title: Priors inside the discriminant scores
study.locator: Section 1.2.2 (posteriors combine class conditionals with P(y = k); LDA adds log P(y = k) to the discriminant) and 1.2.4 (shrinkage as the small-sample stabilizer for those estimates)

focus: sklearn predicts the positive class at 0.5 by default. That bakes in equal costs and matched priors; any asymmetric cost matrix moves the optimal threshold to C_FP/(C_FP + C_FN).
Naive Bayes scores rank well but estimate badly, and OvR margins are not calibrated across classifiers. Thresholding an uncalibrated score encodes its bias as policy.
Priors shift without refitting: multiply the posterior odds by the new-over-old prior-odds ratio. Thresholds move with prevalence even when the feature evidence stays fixed.
units.reproduce: Derive t = C_FP/(C_FP + C_FN) from predicting 1 exactly when p times C_FN exceeds (1 - p) times C_FP, and show costs of 1 and 9 give t = 0.1. From a blank script recompute precisions, recalls and thresholds with precision_recall_curve on binary scores and implement the first-index rule that finds the 90%-precision threshold.
traps: Tuning the threshold on the test set. Thresholds are fitted parameters: select on validation, report once on test, or the reported precision is optimistic.

Comparing thresholds across models with different score scales. A 0.3 cutoff on calibrated probabilities means something different from 3000 on raw margins; compare at matched precision or recall, not matched knob values.
Keeping 0.5 after reweighting classes. Class and sample weights change the score scale and the effective penalty, so retune the threshold after any weighting change.

selfTest.q: False negatives cost 9 times false positives. Which threshold, and why not 0.5?
selfTest.a: t = 1/(1 + 9) = 0.1: predict positive whenever p exceeds 0.1. The 0.5 default assumes equal costs and would miss cheap-to-catch positives.

selfTest.q: Deployment prevalence of positives halves with the same feature evidence. How do the optimal decisions change without refitting?
selfTest.a: Posterior odds halve through the prior-odds ratio, so fewer cases clear any fixed threshold. Recompute posteriors with the new priors and re-derive the threshold instead of reusing the old one.

selfTest.q: Two detectors both report 90% precision, one at margin 3000 and one at probability 0.42. Which threshold is better?
selfTest.a: The knobs are incomparable across scales. Compare recall at matched precision, or expected cost, on the same validation data.

selfTest.q: The guide warns naive Bayes is a bad estimator. What breaks if its raw scores are thresholded at 0.5?
selfTest.a: Ranking can be good while false independence pushes absolute scores to extremes, so 0.5 lands in the wrong place. Set the threshold from measured precision and recall, or calibrate first.
